main_kjv_passage.excerpt: 25. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;

Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.

Practising truth requires more than making a resolution. Small actions cannot earn salvation, yet they can express gratitude for grace and build trustworthy character.

title: The Danger of Loving Money — The Call

7. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.

devotional_message:
God invites us to bring our lives before him without pretending to be perfect. Grace never requires us to conceal wrongdoing; it gives us courage to confess it. Today’s theme matters because the people around us experience the consequences of our choices. An honest heart is ready to be taught by Scripture.

Money is useful, but it is a poor master. Stewardship includes honest income, keeping obligations, providing for needs, and giving without showmanship. Contentment does not forbid saving or sensible planning; it rejects the belief that wealth determines human worth or guarantees God’s approval.

Today’s focus is **the danger of loving money**. That phrase asks a practical question: what would change in your decisions if you took this part of discipleship seriously? A call from God demands a response rather than admiration from a distance. Identify what the teaching asks of you, not merely what it asks of society. An obedient beginning may be simple and costly: an honest conversation, a corrected decision, or an act of service no one notices.

Consider this biblical event: Jesus told a story about a rich farmer whose plans for larger barns overlooked his dependence on God. Read Luke 12:13–21 and reflect on the choices made in the account. The story does not replace the message of the gospel, but it gives us a concrete setting for obedience.

A historical illustration for further checking is this: George Müller organised resources to support the care of orphaned children in Bristol. It is included as a source candidate, not as a verified personal testimony or a claim of miraculous intervention.

Before the day ends, turn the message into one responsible action. If someone has been hurt by your behaviour, acknowledge it and seek appropriate repair. Where safety or serious harm is involved, ask for trustworthy assistance rather than expecting a quick private solution. Pray for the Holy Spirit to guide your conduct in truth and love.

bible_story.title: The Danger of Loving Money — Scriptural illustration
bible_story.narrative: A man asked Jesus to intervene in an inheritance dispute. Jesus warned against covetousness and told a story of a rich landowner whose fields yielded an abundant harvest. Instead of considering God or his neighbours, the farmer planned to pull down his barns and build larger ones to store everything for himself. He imagined many easy years ahead, but God confronted the shortness of his life. Jesus closed by warning against storing up treasure for oneself while neglecting the things of God.
bible_story.spiritual_lesson: Possessions are temporary and cannot secure a person's life; responsible stewardship must be joined to generosity and trust in God.
